Accessibility


Accessibility is a human right and serves everyone

Accessibility is not just about ramps and elevators – it is about making the whole world open and inviting to everyone. Even the digital world. And that is why we aim at making inclusive products and experiences that serve all individuals, regardless of their abilities.
The European Accessibility Act (EAA), introduced in 2019, mandates uniform accessibility standards for digital products and services across the EU by June 28, 2025.
In light of the European Accessibility Act and Telekom's accessibility goals, the ODS components meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) version 2.2, level AA criteria.

Crucial Testing

All the ODS components fulfill WCAG 2.2 A and AA accessibility requirements for the following setup, unless marked otherwise:
For Web

Operating Systems: Windows 10, Windows 11
Browsers: Google Chrome, Official Build, 64 Bit
Screen Reader: NVDA (Version 2023.3.4.31265) and JAWS 2022.2307.1 ILM
Additional tools used for testing the components for Web

Color Contrast Analyzer by TPGi

Google Chrome DevTools (F12)
Browser Zoom 200% and responsive view with at least 320px width (400% Zoom)
Bookmarklets like: Text-Spacing, Highlight H1 – H6 and some internal bookmarklets to page structures.
High contrast mode on Windows
For Mobile

Operating Systems: Android 14 and iOS 17.5.1
Screen Reader: TalkBack on Android and Voiceover on iOS
Additional tools used for testing the components for Mobile

Dark mode on system setting
200% font magnification on system setting
Android Accessibility Scanner
Color Contrast Analyzer by TPGi

External Keyboard
How to achieve full compliance

All the ODS components are compliant with WCAG 2.2 A and AA standards. Each component in ODS comes with their own accessibility considerations within the documentation. But remember, individually accessible components are just one part of building accessible products. To design and build products that anyone can use, refer to ours One Experience accessibility resources. Meanwhile, we recommend you work with an accessibility expert to ensure correct implementation and full compliance of your interfaces and product experience.

Understanding Disabilities

Disabilities can be situational (like bright sunlight making screens hard to read) temporary (such as a broken arm), or permanent (like blindness or paralysis), requiring ongoing accommodation.
When designing for accessibility, it is crucial to consider the following range of disabilities:

Visual Impairments

Visual impairment comes in many forms. It includes conditions such as:

Blindness: Complete or partial absence of vision.
Color blindness: Difficulty distinguishing between certain shades of color, with the most common types being red-green and blue-yellow color deficiencies.
Tunnel vision: Loss of peripheral vision with the central vision remaining intact, like looking through a narrow tube.
Other vision-related problems: Like myopia or astigmatism that require the use of prescription glasses or contact lenses for clear vision.
These individuals might rely on assistive technologies like screen readers, magnification, high contrast, inverted colors for browsing or using digital products.

Digital Product Considerations:

Use alt text for images.
Ensure text contrast.
Avoid relying on color alone.
Enable keyboard navigation.
Provide audio descriptions for videos.
Hearing Impairments

Hearing impairment includes a diverse spectrum of auditory challenges, including conditions like:

Deafness: Complete or nearly complete lack of hearing in one or both ears.
Hard of hearing: Partial hearing loss that may require the use of hearing aids or other assistive devices to amplify sounds.
Tinnitus: A constant or intermittent ringing, buzzing, or other sounds in the ears, which can interfere with clear hearing.
Age-related hearing loss: Gradual loss of hearing that occurs as people get older, typically starting with higher frequencies.
These individuals might rely on assistive technologies like captions, hearing aids, cochlear implants, assistive listening devices, sign language for browsing or using digital products.

Digital Product Considerations:

Provide captions and transcripts.
Use visual/vibrating alerts.
Offer sign language for videos.
Motor Impairments

Motor impairment refers to a range of conditions that affect an individual’s physical ability to move or maintain balance. This category includes diverse motor disabilities, such as:

Paralysis: A loss of muscle function in part of the body that can be complete or partial, temporary, or permanent, and can significantly affect an individual’s mobility and independence.
Cerebral palsy: A group of disorders that affect a person’s ability to move and maintain balance and posture, often caused by developmental brain injuries that occur before, during, or shortly after birth.
Amputation: The loss of a limb or extremity which can profoundly alter a person’s mobility, potentially requiring the use of prosthetics or mobility aids.
Parkinson’s Disease: A progressive neurodegenerative disorder that affects movement, causing tremors, stiffness, and difficulty with balance and coordination.
These individuals might rely on assistive technologies like speech recognition, assistive hardware (e.g., vertical keyboards, sip and puff devices) for browsing or using digital products. Digital Product Considerations:

Ensure keyboard-friendly interactions.
Use visible focus indicators.
Optimize clickable element size and spacing.
Cognitive Impairments

Cognitive impairments encompass a wide range of challenges associated with mental processes such as learning, memory, perception, and problem-solving. Some conditions include:

Learning disabilities: Such as dyslexia, which may pose challenges in reading and interpreting text.
Developmental disorders: Such as autism, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), which can influence attention, memory, and information processing.
Neurodegenerative diseases: Like Alzheimer’s disease and other types of dementia, where progressive cognitive decline can affect memory and problem-solving skills.
Temporary cognitive impairments: States such as grief, intoxication or trauma that can temporarily disrupt cognitive functions, affecting decision-making and memory, for example.
Acquired brain injuries: Conditions like strokes that can result in short-term or long-lasting cognitive changes.
Digital Product Considerations:

Use simple navigation and clear labels.
Employ plain language and good color contrast.
Maintain consistent design and layout.
Minimize flashing animations.
Keep information consistent for memory retention.
For a more detailed introduction to the topic, please read the OneExperience Accessibility Quick-Start Guide.

Suggestions are always welcome

Our goal is to make ODS as accessible as possible. If you have any comments or suggestions on how we can make it better for users living with disabilities, please reach out to our team. For information on contacting the ODS team, see the "Process of getting support" page.
